questions.stem: Which statement describes an undifferentiated, mitosis-capable cell?

options.text: An undifferentiated cell able to divide by mitosis and produce specialised descendants
options.explanation: Undifferentiated plus mitosis plus specialisation potential.

options.text: A fully specialised cell that repairs tissue
options.explanation: Specialised cells are the opposite of stem cells.

options.text: Any cell found in bone marrow
A cell that has stopped dividing

questions.stem: When a stem cell divides, what can its daughters become?

options.text: They merge into one larger cell
They may stay undifferentiated or specialise into particular cell types
They always become specialised immediately
They always remain stem cells

questions.stem: Which statement contrasts adult and embryonic stem cells correctly?

options.text: Embryonic stem cells are found in bone marrow
Both types exist only in embryos
options.explanation: Adult stem cells live in tissues.

options.text: Embryonic stem cells can differentiate into any cell type; adult ones into a limited range
options.explanation: Potency difference is the named contrast.

options.text: Adult stem cells can become any cell type

questions.stem: Where are adult stem cells found, according to the note?

options.text: Only in embryos
Floating freely in the blood
Nowhere after birth
In some tissues and organs, for example the bone marrow
options.explanation: The named location with its example.

questions.stem: Why are embryonic stem cells prized for therapy despite the ethics?

options.text: Because their wider differentiation range lets them become whichever tissue a treatment needs
Because they multiply faster than bacteria
Because they avoid all immune rejection
Because they are the only undifferentiated cells

questions.stem: State the word for a cell that has not yet specialised.
Name the process by which stem cells divide.
questions.modelAnswer: Mitosis — the division route stem cells use.

questions.stem: Explain why bone marrow counts as a stem-cell niche even though blood cells are constantly made there.
questions.modelAnswer: Bone marrow hosts adult stem cells that keep dividing by mitosis, feeding the constant production of blood cells; the tissue's ability to restock red cells, white cells and platelets is exactly the self-renewal-plus-specialisation behaviour that defines a stem-cell population.

questions.stem: A lab brochure claims its cell line 'can become any human cell type'. Which stem-cell class does that describe, and where must the line have come from?
questions.modelAnswer: Any-type potency describes embryonic stem cells, so the line must have originated from embryonic tissue rather than from an adult tissue such as bone marrow.

questions.stem: Which blood products does a bone-marrow transplant restore?

options.text: Plasma proteins only
Red cells, white cells and platelets
Red cells only
Platelets only

questions.stem: Why might a patient's immune system reject donor bone-marrow cells?

options.text: Because donor cells cannot divide
Because marrow cells lack haemoglobin
The donor cells carry different surface antigens from the patient's own
options.explanation: Antigen difference is the named trigger.

options.text: Because donor cells are larger

questions.stem: What advantage do a patient's OWN stem cells have over donor cells?

options.text: They can become any cell type
They are free of ethical objections always
options.explanation: Ethics depends on the source, and adult autologous cells are the uncontroversial case.

options.text: They divide faster than embryonic cells
No rejection and no immunosuppressant drugs needed

questions.stem: Which illness is treated with red blood cells from marrow-derived stem cells?

options.text: Anaemia — the blood cannot carry enough oxygen
Pneumonia
options.explanation: That is a bacterial lung infection.

options.text: Malaria
Diabetes

questions.stem: What is the ethical objection some people raise about embryonic stem cells?

options.text: Embryonic cells cannot specialise
Growing human embryos as a source treats embryos as potential human life to be harvested
options.explanation: The embryo-status concern is the named objection.

options.text: Embryonic cells are expensive to freeze
options.explanation: Cost is not the named objection.

options.text: Embryos divide too slowly

questions.stem: Name the surface proteins whose difference triggers rejection of donor cells.
questions.modelAnswer: Antigens — the surface proteins that mark cell identity.

questions.stem: Name the drugs a patient takes to prevent immune rejection of donor cells.
Explain why white-cell transfusions from marrow-derived stem cells help patients with weakened immune systems.
questions.modelAnswer: White cells such as phagocytes and lymphocytes are the immune system's working cells; a patient with a reduced immune system lacks them, so marrow-derived white cells restore pathogen-fighting capacity directly.

questions.stem: A hospital must choose between donor marrow and the patient's own marrow cells for a transplant. Using this note, state which is safer and give the two-part reason.
questions.modelAnswer: The patient's own marrow cells are safer: they carry the patient's own antigens, so no immune rejection occurs, and the patient avoids immunosuppressant drugs with their infection risks.
